title: Chapter 1: Developer Orientation and the Java Toolchain
description: Establish the workflow used throughout the academy: write source, compile it with a pinned Java 21 JDK, inspect diagnostics and bytecode, launch with an explicit classpath, package a JAR, navigate documentation, and debug from evidence. Extend that workflow to the operating system underneath it (the shell, command syntax, PATH resolution) and to working responsibly with AI coding assistants. Completion means the learner can reproduce the same program from an IDE and terminal, explain every stage between Main.java and a running JVM process, and verify any suggestion before trusting it.

lessons.title: JDK, JVM, JRE, bytecode, and portability
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# JDK, JVM, JRE, bytecode, and portability

## The execution pipeline
Java source is human-readable text. The JDK is the development installation containing javac, java, jar, jshell, and other tools. A runtime environment supplies a JVM plus libraries; a separate historical JRE download is not needed when a JDK is installed. The JVM executes class files on the particular machine.

javac parses source, checks language and type rules, and emits bytecode. The JVM loads classes, verifies their structure, initializes them, and executes methods. Hot code may be compiled into native machine instructions by a just-in-time compiler. A class file is neither Java source nor native Windows executable code.

## Observe the tools
```text
java --version
javac --version
javac --release 21 Main.java
javap -c Main
java Main
```
Run these in the directory containing the previous lesson's Main.java. Both version commands must identify a Java 21 installation for this course. javap shows operations such as obtaining System.out and invoking println; bytecode instructions need not correspond one-for-one to source lines.

## Compatibility and diagnosis
A newer runtime can generally execute older class formats; an older runtime cannot execute newer class formats it does not understand. UnsupportedClassVersionError therefore suggests a compiler/runtime mismatch. Missing libraries can prevent execution even when the class format is compatible.

Portability does not guarantee identical file paths, installed fonts, permissions, locale, or native dependencies. Practice by explaining why a compiled program can run on two operating systems while a hard-coded Windows path fails on one. Record the actual compiler and launcher paths when their versions disagree.

exercises.title: JDK, JVM, JRE, bytecode, and portability: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Which tool translates Java source into class-file bytecode?
hints: javac is the compilation stage that turns source into class-file bytecode; java and jar both operate on class files that already exist.

lessons.title: Compile, launch, classpath, and JAR files
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# Compile, launch, classpath, and JAR files

## Names and locations
A package is part of a class's full name. Create src/academy/Main.java:
```java
package academy;
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Packaged application");
    }
}
```
Compile and launch from the project root:
```text
javac --release 21 -d out src/academy/Main.java
java -cp out academy.Main
jar --create --file academy.jar --main-class academy.Main -C out .
java -jar academy.jar
```
-d selects the compiler's destination. The compiler creates out/academy/Main.class. The classpath contains the root above academy, not the academy directory itself. The fully qualified name is academy.Main. A JAR is an archive of classes and resources; its main-class metadata tells the launcher which entry point to invoke.

## Three different failure stages
A misspelled method causes a compile error. Launching Main instead of academy.Main causes a class-location error. Code that starts and then divides by zero causes a runtime failure. Preserve these distinctions when investigating reports.

A JAR does not automatically contain every external dependency and is not itself a JVM. Executable JAR dependency arrangements vary by build tool. Multiple classpath entries use semicolons on Windows and colons on Unix-like systems.

## Lab
Build from an empty out directory, inspect `jar --list --file academy.jar`, and locate the class and manifest. Move the JAR to another folder and run it. Explain why including src in an archive is different from including compiled classes. Do not delete unrelated directories while cleaning build output.

exercises.title: Compile, launch, classpath, and JAR files: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: out/academy/Main.class exists. Which launch command matches its package?
hints: The classpath root must be the directory that contains the package folder, and the launcher needs the fully qualified name academy.Main, not a file path.

lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# IDE, terminal, JShell, and API documentation

## Use the IDE as a view of the project
Set the project SDK and language level to Java 21, create a conventional source root, and run Main. Locate the IDE's run configuration: main class, working directory, arguments, environment, and classpath. A green Run button may use stale classes or a different SDK from your terminal. The terminal command is an independent reproduction.

Use navigation to find declarations and callers before editing. Rename through the refactoring command so references change together. Format code consistently; formatting cannot determine whether behavior is correct.

## Explore one question in JShell
```text
jshell
jshell> 7 / 2
$1 ==> 3
jshell> 7 / 2.0
$2 ==> 3.5
jshell> /exit
```
JShell accepts expressions and declarations without a full application wrapper. A statement that works in JShell is not necessarily a complete Main.java file. Unless a lesson says “complete program,” later snippets belong inside an appropriate method or class.

## Read an API contract
Look up String.substring in the Java 21 API. Identify the inclusive beginning and exclusive end index, the returned type, and the invalid-index exception. Predict `"Java".substring(1, 3)`: it returns "av". Calling it does not mutate the original String.

## Practice
Run the same application from terminal and IDE, then intentionally change the working directory. Explain why a relative filename may resolve differently. Find one API by its documentation rather than autocomplete and write two legal calls and one illegal call with the expected failure.

exercises.title: IDE, terminal, JShell, and API documentation: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: What does the end index in substring(1, 3) mean?
hints: substring's end index is exclusive: the returned text runs from the start index up to, but not including, that position.

lessons.title: Operating systems, the shell, and the command line
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# Operating systems, the shell, and the command line

## What the operating system is doing while your program runs
When you type `java Main`, the operating system loads the launcher, allocates it a process with its own memory space, schedules its threads onto a CPU core, and provides it a filesystem and a set of open file handles (including standard input, output, and error). The JVM sits on top of this: it asks the OS for memory pages to grow its heap, asks the OS scheduler to run its threads, and asks the filesystem to open the class files it loads. None of this is Java-specific; a Python or C program starting up asks the OS for the same things.

## The shell is a program, not the OS
A terminal window runs a shell: an ordinary program that reads a line of text, splits it into a command and arguments, finds an executable matching the command, and starts it as a new process. On Linux and macOS the common shell is bash or zsh; on Windows it is PowerShell or cmd.exe. The commands differ, but the model is the same everywhere.
```text
Linux/macOS:  ls -la ./src
Windows:      Get-ChildItem -Force .\src
```
`ls`/`Get-ChildItem` is the command; `-la`/`-Force` are options (also called flags) that change its behavior; `./src`/`.\src` is a positional argument naming what to act on. The same three-part shape appears in `javac --release 21 -d out src/Main.java`: `javac` is the command, `--release 21` and `-d out` are options with their own values, and `src/Main.java` is the positional argument being compiled.

## Paths, working directory, and PATH
Every process has a current working directory; a relative path such as `src/Main.java` is resolved against it, which is why running the same command from a different folder can fail to find a file that exists. `PATH` is a separate environment variable listing directories the shell searches when you type a bare command name like `java`; if the JDK's `bin` folder is not on `PATH`, the shell reports the command as not found even though the file exists on disk. This is a different failure from a missing class or a compile error, and it is diagnosed differently: check `PATH` and the installed location, not the source code.

## Practice
Open a terminal in the folder containing an earlier lesson's `Main.java` and run `javac --release 21 Main.java` followed by `java Main` from that directory; then move to the parent directory and run the exact same two commands, predicting and then explaining the failure. List that directory's files with your shell's listing command and identify which part of the command line is the command, which parts are options, and which part is the argument. Print your shell's `PATH` (`echo $PATH` on bash/zsh, `$env:Path` in PowerShell) and locate the directory that contains `java`.

exercises.title: Operating systems, the shell, and the command line: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Typing `java` in a fresh terminal reports "command not found", but the file `java.exe` definitely exists on disk. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The JDK's bin directory is not listed on the PATH environment variable
The source code has a syntax error
hints: A shell only finds bare command names by searching the directories listed in one specific environment variable.

lessons.title: Working with AI coding assistants
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# Working with AI coding assistants

## An assistant suggests; the toolchain confirms
An AI coding assistant can draft a method body, explain an error message, or propose a fix from a stack trace. It cannot compile your program, run your tests, or know whether its suggestion matches your actual requirement; only `javac`, `java`, and a real test case can tell you that. Treat every suggestion as an unverified patch from a collaborator you have not worked with before: read it, understand what each line does, then compile and test it exactly as you would your own code from lesson five's edit-compile-test-debug loop.

## Prompting with the same precision as a bug report
A vague request ("make this faster") produces a vague answer. A useful prompt supplies the same evidence a human reviewer would need: the exact error text and stack trace, the method signature and its contract, a concrete input and the output you expected versus the output you got, and any constraint the solution must respect (no added dependency, must not change a public signature, must handle null). This is the same requirement-gathering discipline from lesson one's receipt example, applied to a conversation instead of a specification document.

## Tool-integrated assistants and accountability
Some assistants can be connected to external tools or data sources through a defined interface, letting them read a file, query a service, or run a command on your behalf rather than only producing text. This does not change who is responsible for the result: an action taken through a tool is still a change to your system, so review what it did (the diff, the command that ran, the file that changed) before trusting it, the same way you would review a script a teammate ran against your machine. Never let an assistant apply a change you have not read, and never paste secrets, credentials, or another person's private data into a prompt.

## Practice
Ask an assistant to implement one function from an earlier chapter's exercise without looking at the reference solution, then compile it, run the existing hidden tests against it by hand, and record every case where the suggestion was wrong or made an unstated assumption. Rewrite one vague prompt ("fix my loop") into a precise one that includes the loop's code, the expected output, and the actual output. Explain, in your own words, why accepting a suggestion you do not understand violates the same principle as pasting code from a forum post without reading it.

exercises.title: Working with AI coding assistants: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: An AI assistant generates a method body that looks reasonable. What establishes whether it is actually correct?
choices: Compiling it and running it against real test cases, the same as any other code
The fact that the assistant is confident in its answer
The suggestion being accepted without changes
hints: Nothing about the source of a suggestion changes how you would normally verify unfamiliar code.

# Chapter 1 assessment

Use the chapter's explanations of the compile-launch pipeline and the exact `public static void main(String[] args)` entry-point signature to solve the decision scenario and repair **A launcher entry point**. Write a prediction of what `javac` and `java` will report before running the debugger, and preserve the required entry-point signature when fixing it.

The function exercise is a bounded practice task, not proof of every chapter competency: it checks a single file-suffix decision, not the whole compile-and-launch workflow. Complete the implementation and external practice described in the seven lessons as well. Review the changed source for why the launcher could not find the entry point, then explain that tradeoff without consulting the answer.

exercises.title: A launcher entry point
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Repair the supplied defect so the program writes exactly `Hello, Java`. The launcher requires the entry point to be declared `public static void main(String[] args)`; the missing `public` modifier means the class compiles but `java` cannot recognize it as a runnable entry point. Preserve the demonstrated `System.out.print` call and explain why restoring the exact signature, rather than hard-coding a print elsewhere, is what makes the class launchable.
hints: The Java launcher needs the public main signature shown in the toolchain lessons.
